findings.title: Comment contradicts threshold condition
findings.explanation: The comment says orders of 500 or more get an extra 5 percent, but the code uses 'subtotal > 500m', so an order of exactly 500 does not receive the bonus. Either the comment or the operator is wrong, and the mismatch can cause incorrect pricing at the boundary.
findings.reason: Identifies the off-by-one boundary: the comment says 500 or more but the code uses > 500, so exactly 500 misses the bonus.

findings.title: Division by zero for empty order
findings.explanation: AveragePricePerItem divides by items.Count without checking for zero. An empty input sequence causes a DivideByZeroException at runtime.
findings.reason: Reports the DivideByZeroException on an empty order at the items.Count division, which is part of label #2.

findings.title: Average divides by line count instead of item count
findings.explanation: The method is named AveragePricePerItem, but it divides the subtotal by the number of order lines, not the total quantity. An order with one line of quantity 10 would be reported as the price of 10 items, not one.
findings.reason: Reports dividing by line count rather than quantity, which is the other half of label #2.

findings.title: No validation of quantities or prices
findings.explanation: Subtotal accepts any quantity and unit price, including negative or zero values. A negative quantity or price silently reduces the total, and null lines cause an unhelpful exception from LINQ.
findings.reason: Speculative input-validation advice. Nothing in this code indicates that negative or null values are expected, and no defect is shown in the pricing logic.

findings.title: Magic numbers for rates and thresholds
findings.explanation: Discount rates (0.10m, 0.05m), the bulk threshold (500m) and the bonus rate are embedded directly in the logic. This makes pricing rules hard to find, review and change.
findings.reason: Style preference about magic numbers. The values are few and readable, and the comment explains the threshold, so this is not a defect.

findings.title: Shipping is charged for empty orders
findings.explanation: Total on an empty line collection yields a discounted total of 0, which is below the free-shipping threshold, so the 7.50 shipping fee is charged for an order with no items.
findings.reason: Charging shipping on an empty order is a speculative business-rule concern. Empty orders are not a meaningful case for Total, and no requirement is violated.

findings.title: SQL injection via unvalidated sortBy in ORDER BY
findings.explanation: The sortBy parameter is interpolated directly into the SQL text with $""" ... {sortBy}. An attacker can supply a value such as 'IssuedOn; DROP TABLE dbo.Invoices--' or a subquery to run arbitrary SQL. Parameters cannot bind column names, so the value must be checked against an allow list.
findings.reason: Identifies SQL injection from unvalidated sortBy interpolated into ORDER BY on line 28.

findings.title: Allow list defined but never used
findings.explanation: SortColumns is declared as a whitelist but SearchAsync never consults it. The protection the code appears to have is therefore absent, which makes the injection risk on line 28 easy to miss in review.
findings.reason: Describes cs-02-invoice-repository#1 but at lines 10-13, outside the window. Describes the same defect from the other side: the allow-list SortColumns is never applied to sortBy, which is the root cause of the injection label.

findings.title: SqlConnection is never disposed in DeleteOlderThanAsync
findings.explanation: The connection is created with plain var and not wrapped in await using, unlike the other method. It is never closed or disposed on the success path or when an exception is thrown, so the pooled connection is held until finalization. Under load this exhausts the connection pool.
findings.reason: Connection in DeleteOlderThanAsync is never disposed, exhausting the pool.

findings.title: Customer search input not validated or escaped
findings.explanation: The customer string is wrapped in % signs and bound with a fixed size of 200. Inputs longer than 198 characters will throw at execution time. LIKE wildcards such as % and _ inside the user input are not escaped, so users can broaden the match unintentionally.
findings.reason: Unescaped LIKE wildcards are a minor but genuine issue; also the NVarChar(200) parameter will truncate rather than throw, so the exception claim is wrong, but the wildcard point stands as a minor real defect.

findings.title: Missing ConfigureAwait(false) in library code
findings.explanation: This is a data access library, and the awaits do not pass ConfigureAwait(false). That forces continuations back onto the captured synchronization context, which can cause deadlocks or unnecessary context switches when callers block on the result.
findings.reason: ConfigureAwait advice is a style/best-practice remark; not a real defect here, and mislabeled as performance.

findings.title: Reset token generated with non-cryptographic Random
findings.explanation: System.Random is a predictable pseudo-random generator. Reset tokens must be unpredictable, so an attacker who observes some output or the seed state can predict valid tokens for other users.
findings.reason: Identifies System.Random as predictable for reset tokens, the same defect as label 1.

findings.title: Token has only about 900,000 possible values and no attempt limiting
findings.explanation: A 6-digit token gives roughly 900k possibilities. Nothing in RedeemAsync limits failed attempts per user, so an attacker can brute-force a token within its 30-minute lifetime.
findings.reason: Flags the six-digit token space as guessable on line 21, which label 1 also names (six digits can be guessed, need enough length).

findings.title: Expiry check is inverted, so expired tokens are accepted
findings.explanation: The condition returns false when ExpiresAt > now, which means it rejects tokens that are still valid and accepts tokens that have already expired. An expired reset token can therefore still reset the password.
findings.reason: Correctly describes the inverted expiry check on line 29.

findings.title: Token is deleted after verification, allowing concurrent reuse
findings.explanation: Two concurrent RedeemAsync calls with the same valid token can both pass the check before either deletes it. Both would return true, so the token is redeemed twice.
findings.reason: Find-then-delete is not atomic, so concurrent redemptions of the same token can both succeed. This is a genuine race that no label covers.

findings.title: Hash comparison is performed after an early return on expiry
findings.explanation: The early return before the constant-time comparison makes the response timing depend on token state. The leak is minor, but mixing the two checks makes the flow harder to reason about.
findings.reason: The early return on expiry reveals nothing exploitable and the finding concedes this. It is a style remark, not a defect.

findings.title: Store interface methods do not accept a CancellationToken
findings.explanation: Async I/O operations cannot be cancelled by callers, which is a common expectation for async APIs in production code.
findings.reason: Missing CancellationToken is a best-practice preference, not a defect here.

findings.title: Awaited calls lack ConfigureAwait(false) in library code
findings.explanation: This is library code, and awaits without ConfigureAwait(false) can capture the synchronization context unnecessarily, which can cause deadlocks in some hosts.
findings.reason: ConfigureAwait advice is a style preference and mostly irrelevant for modern ASP.NET Core hosts.

findings.title: Path traversal via client-supplied file name on upload
findings.explanation: storedName is the raw file.FileName supplied by the client and is combined directly with the uploads folder. A name such as "../../appsettings.json" or an absolute path can write outside the uploads directory, potentially overwriting application files. ASP.NET Core does not sanitize FileName.
findings.reason: Describes the client-supplied file name used as the stored name, which allows path traversal on upload. This is the same defect as label 1.

findings.title: Path traversal in Download via route id
findings.explanation: The id route value is combined into a file path without validation. Values like "..%2F..%2Fappsettings.json" or a rooted path (Path.Combine discards the base when the second argument is rooted) allow reading arbitrary files readable by the process, including secrets in configuration.
findings.reason: Describes path traversal in Download through the unvalidated id, which is label 3.

findings.title: Unnecessary in-memory copy and synchronous I/O in async method
findings.explanation: The upload is copied synchronously into a MemoryStream, then converted with ToArray (another full copy), then written. This doubles memory use per request for up to 10 MB and blocks a thread during the copy. The CancellationToken is also not applied to the copy.
findings.reason: Describes the synchronous CopyTo into a MemoryStream and the buffering of the whole upload, which is label 2.

findings.title: Missing null check on file parameter
findings.explanation: If the request does not include the form field, file may be null, and file.Length on line 16 throws a NullReferenceException that produces a 500 instead of a 400.
findings.reason: The [ApiController] attribute makes model binding and validation return 400 automatically when the required IFormFile is missing. In practice the action is not invoked with a null file.

findings.title: Extension-only file type validation
findings.explanation: Only the file name extension is checked. Any content can be uploaded under a .pdf, .png or .jpg name, and nothing verifies the file signature. Combined with the Download endpoint, which serves files as application/octet-stream, this can be used to store arbitrary content.
findings.reason: Validating only the extension is a genuine weakness: arbitrary content can be stored under an allowed name. It is not covered by any label.

findings.title: Uploads silently overwrite existing files with the same name
findings.explanation: Because the stored name is the client-supplied name, a second upload with the same name replaces the first file without any warning. The returned id then points to different content, which is a data-integrity problem.
findings.reason: Label 1 explicitly includes the overwrite of uploads that share a name, and this finding describes the same overwrite from the same client-supplied name.

findings.title: Hard-coded size text duplicates the constant
findings.explanation: The error message repeats the 10 MB limit as literal text, so it will become wrong if MaxBytes changes. The same limit is also duplicated in the RequestSizeLimit attribute usage.
findings.reason: This is a minor style remark. The message text is not a real defect, and the claim that RequestSizeLimit duplicates the limit is wrong because the attribute uses the constant.

findings.title: Blocking on async call with .Result
findings.explanation: ConvertAsync is declared async but calls GetRateAsync(...).Result, which blocks the calling thread. In contexts with a SynchronizationContext (such as ASP.NET Framework or UI apps) this can deadlock. It also wastes a thread-pool thread during HTTP I/O and ignores the async contract of the method.
findings.reason: Describes blocking .Result inside an async method and the deadlock and thread-waste risks, which is the labeled defect.

findings.title: Cancellation token not propagated through ConvertAsync
findings.explanation: ConvertAsync accepts a CancellationToken but the blocking .Result call hides cancellation semantics, and the token is only passed indirectly. The async method also has no await, so the compiler flags it and the state machine is wasted.
findings.reason: The token is passed directly to GetRateAsync, so the cancellation claim is wrong. The 'no await' remark is only a side effect of the .Result issue, not a separate defect.

findings.title: Shared static Dictionary is not thread-safe
findings.explanation: _rates is a static Dictionary<string, ExchangeRate> that is written in GetRateAsync (line 36) and read concurrently (line 27). Concurrent reads and writes can corrupt the dictionary, cause infinite loops or exceptions, or return inconsistent data. The System.Collections.Concurrent using on line 1 suggests ConcurrentDictionary was intended.
findings.reason: Identifies the static non-thread-safe Dictionary being read and written concurrently.

findings.title: Static cache shared across all instances and ignores injected dependencies
findings.explanation: The cache is static, so every ExchangeRateCache instance shares the same data even though each instance has its own HttpClient and TimeProvider. Tests or multiple tenants with different clocks or endpoints will see each other's cached rates, which makes behavior hard to predict and test.
findings.reason: A static cache shared across instances ignores each instance's injected HttpClient and TimeProvider, so instances with different endpoints or clocks pollute each other. This is a genuine design defect that the labels do not cover.

findings.title: Check-then-act race causes duplicate fetches and stale reads
findings.explanation: The cache is checked on line 27 and written on line 36 with no synchronization. Many concurrent callers for the same expired key will each issue an HTTP request (thundering herd), and a reader can observe a partially updated entry under concurrent writes.
findings.reason: The duplicate-fetch race is mostly benign, and the partially-updated-entry claim comes down to the Dictionary thread-safety problem already labeled. The finding is speculative and overlaps that label.

findings.title: Missing ConfigureAwait(false) on awaited HTTP call
findings.explanation: This is library code that does not need to resume on the caller's synchronization context. Without ConfigureAwait(false), continuations are marshaled back to the captured context, which can cause unnecessary overhead and deadlock risk when combined with blocking callers.
findings.reason: ConfigureAwait advice is a best-practice nit for this code. ASP.NET Core has no sync context, so it does not matter here.

findings.title: Currency codes are not validated
findings.explanation: from and to are used directly to build the cache key and the request URL without validation. Null, empty, or malformed codes produce confusing downstream errors or cache entries with meaningless keys.
findings.reason: Inputs are URL-escaped and bad codes just cause the remote service to fail. This is speculative advice to add validation.

findings.title: Response rate is not validated
findings.explanation: RateResponse.Rate is accepted as-is. A zero, negative, or otherwise implausible rate returned by the remote service would be cached for 10 minutes and used for money conversions in ConvertAsync.
findings.reason: An unvalidated zero or negative rate would be cached and used for money conversions in a payments flow. This is a legitimate robustness gap.

findings.title: No fallback when the rate service fails
findings.explanation: If the HTTP call throws or returns null, the method fails even if a stale cached rate exists. For a payments flow, falling back to a recently expired rate or failing with a clearer error may be preferable, but the current behavior is undefined.
findings.reason: Wanting a stale-cache fallback is a design preference, not a defect in the code.

findings.title: Magic number for currency precision
findings.explanation: The literal 2 in Math.Round encodes an assumption about currency decimal places, which is not true for all currencies (for example JPY uses 0 and some use 3).
findings.reason: Hardcoded 2 decimal places is a minor point and speculative here. It is a style or preference remark rather than a clear defect.

findings.title: Loop performs only two attempts despite MaxAttempts of 3
findings.explanation: The loop condition uses 'attempt < MaxAttempts', so attempts run 1 and 2 only. The constant suggests three total attempts were intended, so the retry budget is one short. The same off-by-one also makes the retry check on line 19 meaningless inside the loop.
findings.reason: Identifies the off-by-one loop condition giving only two attempts instead of three, same as label 1.

findings.title: Non-retryable 4xx errors are retried via HttpRequestException
findings.explanation: EnsureSuccessStatusCode throws HttpRequestException for any non-2xx status, including 400, 401, 404. The catch on line 28 catches that exception while attempt < MaxAttempts and retries it, so permanent client errors are retried needlessly with backoff.
findings.reason: Valid: EnsureSuccessStatusCode throws HttpRequestException on 4xx, and the catch clause retries it while attempt < MaxAttempts, so permanent client errors get retried. Not covered by labels.

findings.title: Final 5xx response yields misleading 'Unreachable' exception
findings.explanation: When the last attempt returns a retryable status (for example 503), the 'continue' is skipped at attempt 2 and the loop ends. Execution then reaches the 'Unreachable' throw, which is reachable and hides the real HTTP failure. The caller gets an InvalidOperationException instead of the status information.
findings.reason: Describes cs-06-shipping-client#1 but at lines 35-35, outside the window. Describes the consequence named in label 1: the last retryable response ends the loop in the 'Unreachable' exception instead of the real error.

findings.title: New HttpClient created per call, bypassing IHttpClientFactory
findings.explanation: Creating and disposing an HttpClient for each request causes socket exhaustion and DNS caching problems under load. It also ignores the injected factory and its configured handlers, timeouts, and resilience settings that GetTrackingStatusAsync uses.
findings.reason: Per-call HttpClient creation causing socket exhaustion and bypassing the factory, same as label 2.

findings.title: Hardcoded API base address
findings.explanation: The shipper endpoint URL is hardcoded in the method. This makes environment changes (staging, sandbox) require code changes and is inconsistent with the 'shipping' named client used elsewhere.
findings.reason: The hardcoded base URL is a legitimate config problem and diverges from the configured 'shipping' client, though it is not the labeled defect.

findings.title: CreateShipmentAsync lacks retry and input validation
findings.explanation: GetTrackingStatusAsync has retry logic while CreateShipmentAsync does not, so behavior is inconsistent. Also, payloadJson is not validated for null or empty before being sent, and the method does not handle cancellation or transient failures in the same way.
findings.reason: Retrying POST creation could cause duplicate shipments; missing retry is not a defect, and the vague validation advice is speculative.

findings.title: Missing ConfigureAwait(false) on await in library code
findings.explanation: This is library code that does not depend on a synchronization context. Awaits on line 26 and elsewhere do not use ConfigureAwait(false), which can cause unnecessary context marshalling and deadlock risk in consumers that block on async calls.
findings.reason: ConfigureAwait(false) advice is a style preference, and the deadlock claim is not a defect in this code.

findings.title: Magic number and no jitter in backoff
findings.explanation: The base delay of 200 is a magic number, and the backoff is deterministic. Multiple clients retrying together can produce synchronized retry storms.
findings.reason: Magic number and missing jitter are minor style and best-practice remarks that do not matter at three attempts.

findings.title: Date range excludes the last day despite the doc comment
findings.explanation: The doc comment says both the first and last day are included, but `end` is `to` at midnight and the filter uses `PlacedAt < end`. Orders placed on the `to` date are silently dropped from the report.
findings.reason: Describes the exclusive end at midnight of the `to` date dropping the last day, contradicting the doc comment.

findings.title: All orders in the range are loaded into memory
findings.explanation: The query materializes every order in the period just to aggregate it in C#. For large date ranges this is slow and memory-heavy, and the aggregation could run in the database.
findings.reason: Loading all orders into memory to aggregate in C# is a genuine performance issue. The label only covers the N+1 customer lookup, though it mentions in-memory loading in passing.

findings.title: N+1 query: one customer lookup per group
findings.explanation: A separate `SingleAsync` round trip runs for every customer group. A report covering many customers issues many queries, and `SingleAsync` also throws if a customer is missing.
findings.reason: Identifies the per-group SingleAsync customer query as an N+1 problem.

findings.title: Average throws on an empty result
findings.explanation: `Enumerable.Average` on an empty sequence throws InvalidOperationException. A customer with no orders causes an unhandled exception instead of a meaningful value.
findings.reason: Identifies Average throwing InvalidOperationException on an empty sequence for a customer with no orders.

findings.title: Hardcoded fallback signing key
findings.explanation: If the Jwt:SigningKey setting is missing, the code silently falls back to a known literal key. Anyone who reads the source can forge JWTs that pass signature validation, which allows authentication bypass in any environment where configuration is incomplete.
findings.reason: Identifies the hardcoded fallback signing key on line 11 that allows forged tokens.

findings.title: Token lifetime validation disabled
findings.explanation: ValidateLifetime = false means expired tokens are accepted indefinitely. A leaked or stolen token stays valid forever, and ClockSkew on line 24 has no effect.
findings.reason: Identifies ValidateLifetime = false, so expired tokens are accepted.

findings.title: Bearer token written to logs
findings.explanation: The full Authorization header, which contains the bearer token, is logged on every authentication failure. Log readers, log aggregators, or anyone with log access could replay live tokens.
findings.reason: Identifies the Authorization header and bearer token being logged on authentication failure.

findings.title: Issuer and audience may be null without validation
findings.explanation: ValidateIssuer and ValidateAudience are enabled, but ValidIssuer and ValidAudience are read from configuration with no null or empty check. A missing setting produces a misconfigured validator that rejects all tokens or behaves unpredictably, and the error appears only at runtime.
findings.reason: With a missing issuer or audience and validation enabled, tokens are rejected (fail closed), which is not a security hole. The speculative configuration-validation advice is not a real defect here.

findings.title: No argument null checks
findings.explanation: The services and configuration parameters are used without null guards. A null argument causes a NullReferenceException later, which is harder to diagnose than an ArgumentNullException at the entry point.
findings.reason: Null guards on an extension method called at startup are a style preference with little practical value.

findings.title: string.Normalize can throw on malformed input
findings.explanation: string.Normalize throws ArgumentException when the input contains invalid Unicode, such as unpaired surrogates. ToSlug only guards against null, so user-supplied titles with malformed characters will raise an unhandled exception.
findings.reason: string.Normalize throws ArgumentException on invalid Unicode such as lone surrogates. ToSlug only guards null, so malformed user titles would throw unexpectedly. It is a low-severity edge case, but the claim is accurate.

findings.title: Entire title is normalized even though output is capped at MaxLength
findings.explanation: Normalize(FormD) allocates and processes the full input string, which can be arbitrarily long, even though the loop stops after 80 output characters. The work is wasted for long titles.
findings.reason: This is a speculative micro-optimization. Normalizing the whole string is linear and simple, and the finding gives no evidence that long titles are a real problem here.

findings.title: Redundant truncation and TrimEnd
findings.explanation: The loop already breaks once the length reaches MaxLength, so the Math.Min in ToString is a no-op. Hyphens are only appended before a letter or digit, so the result can never end with a hyphen and TrimEnd('-') never removes anything. These calls suggest the logic is less clear than it is.
findings.reason: The claim is wrong. When the slug is at 79 characters with a pending hyphen, one iteration appends both a hyphen and a letter, reaching 81. So Math.Min truncation is needed. Truncating to 80 can also leave a trailing hyphen, so TrimEnd is needed too.

findings.title: Nullable column read with GetString may throw
findings.explanation: reader.GetString(2) throws SqlNullValueException if the Email column is NULL. The code never checks reader.IsDBNull, and the Customer record declares Email as non-nullable. If the schema allows NULL emails, FindAsync will fail at runtime for those rows.
findings.reason: Speculative: the schema is unknown and the record's non-nullable Email suggests a NOT NULL column. Without evidence of a nullable column this is not a defect.

findings.title: Name length not validated against NVarChar(200)
findings.explanation: The parameter is declared as NVarChar with size 200, but the input is only checked for whitespace. A name longer than 200 characters after trimming will cause a SqlException from the database layer instead of a clear argument error.
findings.reason: A SqlParameter with size 200 does not throw; SQL Server raises a truncation error (or truncates silently). Failing on over-long input is acceptable behavior, so this is a minor 'consider adding' remark, not a defect.

findings.title: Awaits lack ConfigureAwait(false) in library code
findings.explanation: This is a data-access library, and none of its awaits use ConfigureAwait(false). Continuations are therefore forced back to the caller's synchronization context, which can add overhead and cause deadlocks in UI or legacy ASP.NET callers that block on the result.
findings.reason: ConfigureAwait(false) is a best-practice preference. Modern ASP.NET Core has no synchronization context, and the deadlock only affects callers who block on the result, so it is not a defect in this code.

findings.title: Subject claim lookup may fail under default JWT claim mapping
findings.explanation: ASP.NET Core's JWT handler maps inbound claims by default, and 'sub' is commonly remapped to ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier. User.FindFirst("sub") can then return null even for authenticated users, causing every request to fail.
findings.reason: In ASP.NET Core 8+, JsonWebTokenHandler (the default) does not remap inbound claims, so 'sub' stays 'sub'. Even in the older handler, mapping is a configuration matter, and the code is plausible as written. Speculative.

findings.title: Missing subject claim surfaces as HTTP 500
findings.explanation: Throwing InvalidOperationException for a missing claim produces an unhandled server error. An authenticated request without the expected claim is a client or identity-configuration problem, so it should not be reported as a server fault.
findings.reason: An authenticated token lacking the required subject claim is a server or identity configuration fault, so throwing and returning 500 is defensible. The finding is a preference remark.

findings.title: Required SKU accepts whitespace-only values
findings.explanation: [Required] rejects null and empty strings but accepts whitespace, so a SKU such as "   " passes validation and reaches the service layer.
findings.reason: [Required] on a string rejects null and empty, and AllowEmptyStrings is false by default, which also rejects whitespace-only strings. The claim is factually wrong.

findings.title: No idempotency protection for order placement
findings.explanation: POST creates a new order on every call. A client retry after a timeout or network failure can create duplicate orders with no way to detect them.
findings.reason: Idempotency keys are a speculative best-practice suggestion, not a defect in this code.
